summary: This standards-track document specifies how Ethernet VPN can be used as a network virtualization overlay for data centers. It examines tunnel encapsulation options over IP, including VXLAN, NVGRE and MPLS over GRE, and how they affect the EVPN control plane and procedures.

eli5.summary: Many private networks can share the same wires, each in its own pretend tunnel. This explains how to build that using a standard address-sharing system.

subtitle: How Ethernet VPN's BGP control plane can drive VXLAN, NVGRE and MPLS-over-GRE overlays in multi-tenant data centers.

tldr.problem: A multi-tenant data center needs isolated tenant networks, very many tenants, Layer 2 reach across the data center and between data centers, and free VM movement, over a plain IP underlay.
tldr.mechanism: EVPN's BGP control plane is reused with IP tunnel encapsulations. The VNI or VSID rides in the field that normally holds an MPLS label, a BGP Encapsulation Extended Community names the encapsulation, and new multihoming procedures such as local-bias split-horizon replace features that relied on MPLS.
tldr.outcome: EVPN can serve as a network virtualization overlay solution with VXLAN, NVGRE and MPLS over GRE. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9746.

today: RFC 8365 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9746. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: EVPN as a Network Virtualization Overlay
sections.content:
This document specifies how Ethernet VPN (EVPN, RFC 7432) can be used as a Network Virtualization Overlay (NVO) solution. An NVO addresses the needs of a multi-tenant data center, especially one with virtualized hosts such as virtual machines. It analyzes three IP tunnel encapsulations: VXLAN (RFC 7348), NVGRE (RFC 7637) and MPLS over GRE (RFC 4023). It says the specification also applies to GENEVE, with some incremental work left to a separate document.

Following RFC 7364, the key requirements are isolation of traffic per tenant, support for a large number of tenants (tens or hundreds of thousands), Layer 2 connectivity within a tenant segment across Points of Delivery or data centers, and the ability for a VM to move between physical points of attachment. The underlay is assumed to give IP connectivity between NVO endpoints.

The document also adds new multihoming procedures for split-horizon filtering and mass withdrawal, EVPN route construction for VXLAN and NVGRE, and ASBR procedures for multihomed Network Virtualization Edge (NVE) devices.
sections.eli5: A big building holds many companies. Each needs its own private network even though the cables are shared, and this document shows how to do it with a system that already exists.

sections.title: The EVPN Features Being Reused
sections.content:
The RFC lists the EVPN attributes that address control-plane scaling and ease of deployment. The main ones are:

  • Control-plane information is distributed with BGP, and broadcast and multicast traffic uses a shared multicast tree or ingress replication.
  • MAC and IP addresses are learned in the control plane rather than the data plane, so unknown unicast and ARP frames need not be flooded.
  • Route Reflectors cut a full mesh of BGP sessions down to one session per PE.
  • Auto-discovery via BGP finds participating PEs, redundancy groups, tunnel encapsulation types and multicast members.
  • All-Active multihoming lets a CE use several links to several PEs, and a single route withdrawal (mass withdrawal) lets PEs drop a failed link as next hop for all its MAC addresses.
  • Route Targets define topologies such as mesh, hub and spoke, and extranets.

Because the NVO design goal is millions of instances per common physical infrastructure, control-plane scaling is described as extremely important.
sections.eli5: Instead of every machine shouting to find its neighbours, they all post notes on a shared board. That scales much better.

sections.title: Encapsulation Options
sections.content:
VXLAN and NVGRE both carry an identifier of the NVO instance in every packet: the VNI in VXLAN and the VSID in NVGRE. The RFC uses VNI for both. A PE is equivalent to an NVE or VTEP.

VXLAN is based on UDP, with an 8-byte header after the UDP header and a 24-bit VNI that typically maps one-to-one to the tenant VID. In that mode the ingress VTEP adds no inner VLAN tag and the egress VTEP discards frames that have one, which matches VLAN-Based Service in RFC 7432. If configured, an inner VLAN tag may be included, which maps to VLAN Bundle Service. NVGRE is based on GRE and mandates the optional GRE Key field, which carries the VSID. An inner VLAN tag is prohibited.

EVPN routes are encoded as before, except that the BGP Encapsulation Extended Community from RFC 5512 marks the encapsulation type. For MPLS over GRE, the EVPN MPLS client layer is carried over an IP tunnel transparently, so EVPN procedures are not affected. The GRE key field should be present, giving a 32-bit entropy value, only if the P nodes can do ECMP hashing on it. The Checksum and Sequence Number fields MUST NOT be included.
sections.eli5: The tunnel is like an envelope with a tenant number on it. Different envelope types exist, but they all say whose mail is inside.

sections.title: Identifiers, EVIs and BGP Routes
sections.content:
A VNI is defined as a 24-bit globally unique value, but a locally significant one can be better for data-center interconnect. With a Gateway at the data-center edge, the Gateway translates VNIs between each data center and the WAN. Without a Gateway, the VNI used by the sender is allocated by the receiving NVE, much like a downstream-assigned MPLS label.

As in RFC 7432, there are two ways to map broadcast domains to an EVI. Option 1 uses a single broadcast domain per EVI, with an RD and RT per VNI. It allows BGP RT constraints to limit route distribution, but may add provisioning work unless RD and RT are derived from the VNI. Option 2 puts multiple VNIs in one EVI (the VLAN-aware bundle service). It needs no per-VNI RD and RT, but routes may be imported by NVEs that do not care about a VNI.

To ease configuration for Option 1, the 6-octet RT can be auto-derived from a 2-octet AS number, a one-bit A field, a 3-bit Type, a 4-bit domain-id and a 3-octet Service ID. For 4-octet AS numbers the RT must be configured manually.

In routes, the MPLS label fields of the MAC/IP Advertisement, Ethernet A-D per EVI and IMET (PMSI Tunnel attribute) routes carry the 24-bit VNI. The Ethernet Tag MUST be zero for VLAN-Based Service. The Next Hop MUST be the IPv4 or IPv6 address of the NVE.
sections.eli5: Every tenant gets a number. Some places use one global list of numbers, and others let each receiver hand out its own, like coat-check tickets.

sections.title: Mixing Encapsulations
sections.content:
The Encapsulation Extended Community tells each NVE which encapsulations every other NVE in an EVI supports. An ingress NVE can send to an egress NVE only if their sets overlap, and it chooses from the overlap. If the community is absent, default MPLS or a locally configured encapsulation is assumed.

A PE that advertises several encapsulations MUST advertise only ones that use the same EVPN procedures, including split-horizon filtering. VXLAN and NVGRE (or MPLS and MPLS over GRE) can be advertised together. A PE MUST NOT advertise VXLAN and MPLS together, because the MPLS field holds either a label or a VNI but not both, and some procedures differ.

The operator of an EVI must make sure all NVEs share at least one encapsulation, or service may be disrupted. The community lets a violation be detected, but what to do about it is outside the document.
sections.eli5: Two people can only talk if they share a language. Each announces which ones it speaks, and the sender picks one they both know.

sections.title: Single-Homed and Multihomed NVEs
sections.content:
When the NVE sits in a hypervisor, hosts are typically not multihomed, so multihoming routes and procedures are not needed. Four of the eight EVPN route types and attributes remain: MAC/IP Advertisement, Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag, MAC Mobility and Default Gateway. A single-homing ingress NVE should still process Ethernet A-D per ES and per EVI routes to benefit from fast convergence, Aliasing and Backup Path when talking to multihomed egress NVEs.

When the NVE is in a ToR switch with multihomed servers, the full set of routes is used. In Single-Active mode, Aliasing is not required, split-horizon may not be, and the other functions still are. In All-Active mode the encapsulation affects split-horizon and Aliasing, which rely on the MPLS client layer.

MPLS EVPN uses an ESI label for split-horizon. VXLAN and NVGRE have no such label, so the RFC recommends Local Bias. Each NVE tracks the IP addresses of the NVEs it shares multihomed segments with, filters multi-destination frames whose tunnel source is one of them on the shared segments, and the ingress NVE replicates locally to all directly attached segments. Only one IP address per NVE is needed. A segment MUST NOT mix MPLS-over-GRE split-horizon with local-bias NVEs. Aliasing and Backup Path use the same Ethernet A-D per EVI route as in MPLS, with Ethernet Tag and VNI set as in the route construction rules.
sections.eli5: If a kid has two doors into the house, the message must not come in through one and then loop out through the other. Local Bias is the rule that stops that.

sections.title: Multicast and Data-Center Interconnect
sections.content:
For multicast, the IMET route discovers the multicast tunnels for an EVI. Its PMSI Tunnel attribute carries the tunnel type and identifier, and the Encapsulation Extended Community says which encapsulation that tunnel uses. For VXLAN and NVGRE, tunnel types 3 (PIM-SSM), 4 (PIM-SM), 5 (BIDIR-PIM) and 6 (Ingress Replication) can be used. With globally assigned VNIs, each PE MUST advertise an IMET route for ingress replication or PIM-SSM, and MAY for PIM-SM or BIDIR-PIM.

For data-center interconnect over an MPLS/IP core, two scenarios are considered. With Gateways, EVPN routes end at the Gateway, so NVEs only keep local routes when default IP and unknown MAC routes are used, and failures converge faster because withdrawals do not reach remote data centers. With ASBRs (inter-AS Option B), DCI devices keep no MAC or IP tables and need locally assigned VNIs that act like 24-bit VPN labels.

The ASBR next-hop rewrite breaks per-ES mass withdrawal, because a remote PE cannot tie the Ethernet A-D per ES route to MAC routes. Aliasing still works. So mass withdrawal falls back from per-ES to per-EVI: a detached PE MUST withdraw its Ethernet A-D per EVI routes too, and a remote PE SHOULD then remove it as next hop for that segment's MACs. It converges more slowly than per-ES, but much faster than per-MAC.
sections.eli5: When the networks of two buildings are joined, the guard at the border changes the return address on every letter. So the system uses a slightly slower way to tell everyone a door is broken, but it still works.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The document uses IP-based tunnels for the data plane, so the security considerations of those tunnel technologies apply, including those in RFC 7348 and RFC 7637. As with RFC 5512, altering the information used to build encapsulation headers or choose a tunnel type or tunnel may cause user packets to be misrouted, misdelivered or dropped. BGP's own security considerations, in RFC 4271 and RFC 4272, apply equally.

IANA registered five values in the BGP Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute Tunnel Types registry: 8 for VXLAN, 9 for NVGRE, 10 for MPLS, 11 for MPLS in GRE and 12 for VXLAN GPE.
sections.eli5: If someone tampers with the envelope instructions, letters can go to the wrong place. So the usual safety rules for the tunnels and for BGP still apply.
